---
title: "Biodiversity means life"
author: "Owen Petchey"
date: 2026-09-18
categories: [outreach, public engagement, biodiversity]
image: cover.jpg
---

Most of the biodiversity that keeps us alive is invisible to the naked eye. Owen's own way of making that point in public talks and workshops is a lab coat hung with dozens of plush microbes and cells — bacteria, protists, viruses, neurons — worn while explaining just how much of the living world working on our behalf never gets seen, let alone thanked.

That's also the premise behind [*"Biodiversity means Life"*](https://www.gcb.uzh.ch/en/Agora.html){target="_blank"}, an AGORA public-engagement project run by the University Research Priority Programme in Global Change and Biodiversity (URPP GCB) at UZH. The project takes the form of a travelling tent kitted out with interactive, hands-on exhibits, through which GCB scientists and students talk with the general public about the critical roles biodiversity plays in our lives — and about global change and its consequences for that biodiversity — in terms that don't require a science background to follow.

One concrete outing for this kind of engagement was the *MikroMakro Parcours*, part of a public exhibition at the Kunsthalle Zürich (Löwenbräu-Areal) running from 25 August to 4 November 2018, where GCB researchers spoke with visitors about their biodiversity and global change research as part of the wider programme. It's the same spirit as the plush-microbe coat: biodiversity is easiest to care about once you can actually see — or wear — the parts of it that usually stay hidden.
